card.hook: Picture a whole row of pale 18th-century palaces, then picture them again, upside down, in a sheet of water barely thicker than a puddle. That's the trick Bordeaux plays on you here, and it works best when the water goes still.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the Miroir d'eau pool, and face the Bourse façades across the water. Keep the central façade in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which keeps the façades looking natural. If you can't fit the whole front and its reflection in, tap zoom 0.5x. Save zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the sculptures and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the façade, then slide it a little darker so the floodlit stonework doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Early morning is calmest and quietest for the mirror shot. Dusk or blue hour is the one for the floodlit reflection. One guide says the water cycle runs roughly every 15 to 20 minutes, so wait for the calm phase if you want the mirror.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the wet paved slab between Quai de la Douane and Quai Louis XVIII, with the Palais de la Bourse façades behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low so the mirrored façades fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the riverside quay near L'Estacade restaurant and aim toward Place de la Bourse, with the Fountain of the Three Graces centred, and to wait for a tram to pass before shooting.
card.rules_and_safety: The water mirror is slippery (one local photo guide warns 'Attention, ça glisse!'), and the granite can be slick when misty, so walk slowly. The pool is drained in the coldest winter months, and guides disagree on the exact season, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Crouch low, hold your phone just above the water, and get the façade and its twin in one frame, with zero wet knees if you can manage it.
card.good_to_know: Place de la Bourse was built between 1730 and 1775 by Jacques Gabriel and his son Ange-Jacques Gabriel, who finished the work. The Palais de la Bourse on the north side is now the Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and the former Hôtel des Fermes on the south side houses the National Museum of Customs. The area has been part of Bordeaux's UNESCO World Heritage listing since 2007.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the Miroir d'eau pool, and face the Bourse façades across the water. Keep the central façade in the middle of your screen.

card.hook: Picture a giant carafe of wine swirling beside the river, and you've got the Cité du Vin. The building is the star here, so let it have the whole stage.
card.stand_here: Stand on Esplanade de Pontac, the public square in front of the main entrance, and face the building. You'll get the whole curved shape with the Garonne behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the full building and the river in one frame. Try 0.5x only if you want a dramatic close-up, and watch the edges for stretching. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for facade details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the building on one side of the frame, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Low tide shows sandbanks in the river, which look great in the foreground, so check tide times. Early or late in the day usually gives softer light on the building.
card.selfie_here: Try the Gina rooftop bar on top of the Renaissance Bordeaux hotel. Its open terrace stretches over the Bassins à flot with the museum across the water, so use the front camera (0.5x if you want more in), and keep the building over your shoulder. card.good_to_know: The Cité du Vin is Bordeaux's wine museum. It was designed by XTU Agency, led by Anouk Legendre and Nicholas Desmazières, and opened on 1 June 2016. It had passed 2 million visitors by May 2022.

card.hook: Picture an 18th-century palace standing on its own upside-down twin, all in about 2 cm of water. Then a cloud of mist rolls in and wipes the picture clean. That's the Miroir d'eau, and you get two photos for the price of one.
card.stand_here: Head for Place de la Bourse, then walk to the Garonne quay side of the pool and turn round to face the Bourse façades. From there the buildings, the thin sheet of water and the symmetry of the square all fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full façades and their reflection in one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched view, and try 2x for details like people wading through the mist.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the façade with the middle of the screen so the reflection looks balanced, then crouch and hold the phone just above the water to make the reflection bigger.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the water is calm and there are fewer people. Sunset or after dark is lovely too, with lit façades and golden reflections (use night mode once it's dark).
card.selfie_here: Wade into the shallow water on the Quai de la Douane side of the Miroir d'eau and turn so the Palais de la Bourse is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the façade, and let the reflections surround you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Place de la Bourse side, facing across the pool, so the whole mirror fits in the frame while you pose out in the water.
card.rules_and_safety: The pool only runs for part of the year, so check the official site before you go. The pavement can be slippery when it's wet, so pack spare clothes, especially for children.
card.challenge: Take the same façade twice, once with a sharp, mirror-perfect reflection and once with the mist drifting through, then see which one wins.
card.good_to_know: The Miroir d'eau covers 3,450 square metres and was built in 2006, designed by landscape artist Michel Corajoud. It's granite slabs under about 2 cm of water, and every 15 minutes a mist rises and softens the whole scene. It's described as the most-photographed place in Bordeaux's Port of the Moon.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Place de la Bourse, then walk to the Garonne quay side of the pool and turn round to face the Bourse façades. From there the buildings, the thin sheet of water and the symmetry of the square all fit in one frame.

card.hook: The Grosse Cloche is an old town gate with a bell tower on top, and it's got a face: a big clock, right there on show. From this wide avenue you get the whole front of it, with more elbow room than in the narrow old-town streets.
card.stand_here: Stand on Cours Victor Hugo, on the side where you can see the clock face. From here the gate lies to the north, so face north and you'll have its full front in view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole gate and the clock face. If traffic or people stop you stepping back, switch to 0.5x, but keep the gate away from the edges of the screen. Then try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) for a close-up of the clock and the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the two sides of the arch up with the vertical lines so the gate stands straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. Skip noon on the first Sunday of the month if you want a quiet street, because the bell may draw a crowd.
card.selfie_here: Try Place Saint-James, the small square right next to the Grosse Cloche, which gives a close-up view of it. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the tower sits behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a little way down Rue Saint-James on the south side, looking up the street, while you stand in front of the tower so it fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stand where people can still walk past, and don't block residents, shops or anyone on the move. Never step into traffic to get a symmetrical shot of the tower.
card.challenge: Take the same gate three ways: the full front at 1x, a clock-face close-up, and one from Rue Saint-James between the old-town façades. Then pick a winner.
card.good_to_know: The bell is said to ring at noon on the first Sunday of the month and on a few special occasions. Going inside the tower is a separate guided visit, not an open viewing platform, so take your photos from the street. Check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.

card.hook: Stand at the top of Rue Sainte-Catherine and the whole street seems to pour away from you, shopfronts and strollers all the way down. It's about 1.2 km long, so you won't fit it all in one shot, but the first view is a cracker.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place de la Comédie, at the north end where the street begins beside the Grand Théâtre. Face south, with the theatre behind you, and keep to the middle of the street's line so the façades lean in evenly on both sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the long street with the Grand Théâtre behind you. Try zoom 0.5x for more of those grand façades, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to squeeze the crowd and shopfronts together down the avenue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the façades so the buildings stand up straight, then tap the middle of the street and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Market days and the sales in February and July can fill the street and block your view. One guide says evening light falls better down the cross streets than at midday.
card.selfie_here: Try Porte Dijeaux, the neoclassical gate with Corinthian columns, which is close to Rue Sainte-Catherine rather than on it. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the gate over your shoulder. One guide says sunrise gives the best light there. Back on the street, the Dames de France building has rounded, domed corners you can spot from far off, so look up and let it frame you.
card.rules_and_safety: Shop entrances are private, so step aside if staff ask. One street-photography guide advises watching your bag in crowds, including here.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the street shrinks to a tiny point behind you, with not a single person looking at the camera. Bonus points if it's busy.
card.good_to_know: The street follows the line of the old Roman cardo and became fully pedestrian in 1984. It was refurbished between 2000 and 2003 by Jean-Michel Wilmotte. Halfway along, Place Saint-Projet has a fountain made around 1715, and where the street meets Cours Alsace-Lorraine a bas-relief on the ground marks two underground rivers, the Peugue and the Devèze.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place de la Comédie, at the north end where the street begins beside the Grand Théâtre. Face south, with the theatre behind you, and keep to the middle of the street's line so the façades lean in evenly on both sides.

card.hook: Two pointy turrets, a slate spire and not one car in your shot: Porte Cailhau is a gate that looks like it's showing off, and Place du Palais gives it the stage.
card.stand_here: Head for Place du Palais, about 87 m south-west of the gate, on the river side, and about a minute or two on foot. Face the gate so you see the whole front, with the pointed archway in the middle.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the whole gate fits with a bit of sky above the spire. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the statue, the turrets and the pointed arch. Use 0.5x only if you move in close or want the quayside buildings in the picture.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, line the archway up with the middle of the frame so the two turrets sit evenly on each side, and hold the phone level so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning, about 7:30 to 9:00 in spring and autumn, is the sweet spot: the square is quieter and the light is soft on the stone. A dusk shot from the square or the quay is also possible, so try night mode and rest your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the paved square in Place du Palais with the gate and its towers behind you, and the cafe terraces beside you for a bit of atmosphere. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the gate rise over your shoulder. For a second go, try Quai Richelieu on the Garonne side with the gate behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the square facing the gate's front while you stand in front of the gate, and ask them to go wide (0.5x) so the towers and spire both fit in, because the square is quite confined.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed inside the gate, but skip the flash so you don't disturb other visitors. Going inside is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get both turrets perfectly even in your frame, then zoom in and catch King Charles VIII on the front without losing the arch.
card.good_to_know: Porte Cailhau was built between 1493 and 1496 as part of the old city walls. The walls have gone, but you can still see where they joined the gate at the back. The statue on the front is King Charles VIII, and the gate was partly built to mark his victory at the Battle of Fornovo in 1495. It has been a protected historical monument since 1883.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the monument, the square and the trees together. Switch to 1x for a natural view of the column and fountain, then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close shots of the horses.

card.best_time: Daylight is easiest for the outside. In the morning or late afternoon the lower sun usually gives the stonework more shape.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the long front of the museum over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher than your face so more of the building squeezes in.
card.rules_and_safety: If you want to take photos inside, the rules can differ from room to room, so ask at the desk.
card.challenge: Get all 143 m of the building in one shot with the sides perfectly straight, and no leaning allowed.
card.good_to_know: The building went up in the 1880s as the Faculty of Letters and Sciences, designed by the municipal architect Charles Durand. The museum moved in on 9 January 1987. Inside are more than 70,000 pieces, including the Venus of Laussel and the cenotaph of Michel de Montaigne.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Musée d'Aquitaine, then walk out to the edge of the building and turn to look back at it. Keep stepping back until the whole long front fits, with a bit of street in the frame.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the Musée d'Aquitaine behind the visitor, or a passer-by spot for photographing the whole building, so I have left both empty rather than guess. The Bordeaux Tourism pages (bordeaux-tourism.co.uk) describe the facade's monumental steps and visitors 'in the square', but they do not name the square. Gironde Tourisme places the museum 350 meters from Place Pey-Berland and Saint-André Cathedral, and Le Map Bordeaux lists Place Pey-Berland only as nearby sightseeing. Neither source calls either place a photo spot, so I did not use them. The museum is at 20 Cours Pasteur, and I found no page that gives a selfie-stick or tripod rule or a safety point. Photography without flash is generally permitted, but restrictions may apply in temporary exhibitions (audiala.com); this is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so it is not listed under rules. The coordinates in the request were not checked against any page.

card.hook: The bell tower here doesn't sit on the church. It stands on its own next to it, like it wanted a bit of personal space. That odd pairing is why Bordeaux Cathedral is so easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Pey-Berland, in front of the west façade, and face the cathedral. It lies to the east, straight ahead of you, with the separate Pey-Berland bell tower beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole façade and the tower in one frame. If it won't all fit, tap 0.5x instead of stepping back into the tram lines. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved stonework and the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and keep your phone upright, not tilted up, so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Early evening, when warm light falls on the stone.
card.selfie_here: Grab a café table on Place Pey-Berland, directly across from the north side of the cathedral, and use the front camera with the cathedral over your shoulder. Try 0.5x to squeeze more of it in. The café isn't named, so find the terrace by its position on the square.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street at the Gambetta tram stop (Line B), a few blocks from the cathedral, where the buildings on both sides frame the whole cathedral.
card.rules_and_safety: Trams run through the square, so listen for them before you step out for a photo. The outside is photographed from open public squares. Inside, photos are allowed without flash but not during Mass. The tower climb is paid, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Leave a strip of square and tram lines at the bottom of your photo, then wait for a stranger to stroll into it for instant scale.
card.good_to_know: A church of Saint-André is first recorded here in 814, and the earlier Romanesque church was consecrated in 1096. In 1137 Eleanor of Aquitaine married the future Louis VII of France in the cathedral. The bell tower was begun in 1440 and finished in 1500, and UNESCO lists the cathedral among the Bordeaux churches on the Routes of Santiago de Compostela.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place Pey-Berland, in front of the west façade, and face the cathedral. It lies to the east, straight ahead of you, with the separate Pey-Berland bell tower beside it.

card.hook: Most people shoot Place des Quinconces from the middle and wonder why it feels so empty. Walk to the river and look back, and the whole tree-lined expanse suddenly makes sense, with the monument tiny and far away at the end of it.
card.stand_here: Go to Quai Louis XVIII, on the riverside promenade on the Garonne bank, east of the square. Face west, with the Monument aux Girondins straight ahead across the open space. From the monument it's about 5 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole square in. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the monument closer. Save zoom 0.5x for when you're standing much nearer the rostral columns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the monument on one of the vertical lines and let the tree lines lead your eye to it, then tap the monument and slide a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Morning is likely to be easiest, because the sun will be behind you as you face west. In the evening you'll be shooting toward the light. Rides, a Ferris wheel, circus tents or a Christmas market can fill the square in some seasons, so check what's there when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Climb to the steps of the Monument aux Girondins and turn so the column and fountain are behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and walk around the monument to find your best angle. The fountain basins at the base are another good backdrop. It's worth a quick check on site that the angle works.
card.rules_and_safety: The Bordeaux tourism office doesn't recommend climbing the monumental statues, so keep your selfie to the steps.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the monument is so small and far away that your friend has to guess what it is.
card.good_to_know: The trees were planted in 1818 in staggered rows called quincunxes, which gave the square its name, and the square itself was laid out in 1820. The Monument aux Girondins is 54 metres tall and was built between 1894 and 1902. The fountain's statues were removed in 1942, then recovered, restored and put back in 1983.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to Quai Louis XVIII, on the riverside promenade on the Garonne bank, east of the square. Face west, with the Monument aux Girondins straight ahead across the open space. From the monument it's about 5 minutes on foot.

card.hook: Plot twist: the Pont de pierre is called the stone bridge, but it's mostly brick. Better still, its 17 arches march across the Garonne like they were made for your phone screen.
card.stand_here: Head to Quai de Queyries on the right bank (rive droite) of the Garonne, in the Bastide district. Turn around and face back across the river at the bridge, with the Saint-Michel spire poking up past the far end.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole row of arches fits in one shot. Then try zoom 2x to pull the Saint-Michel spire in closer behind the bridge. Save zoom 0.5x for the closer quayside spots.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, sit the bridge along the lower third, then tap the bridge and slide to darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunrise and sunset give soft light from the riverbanks. Early morning is also likely to be quieter on the quay, and after dark, night mode and a steady lean on a railing keep the lights sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge walkway at sunset, facing the quays and the Saint-Michel spire. A local shooting guide calls it a classic couples' spot, with arches and lampposts. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the view over your shoulder. No page confirmed a shot with the bridge right behind you, so check the framing on your screen before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on Quai des Queyries, on the right bank, to face the bridge so the whole span and the Saint-Michel basilica are in their frame, while you stand a little way along the quay in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is being renovated over several years, so expect scaffolding, fencing or temporary cycle and pedestrian lanes. Check the official site for closures or diversions before you go.
card.challenge: Keep the horizon dead level, then wait for a tram or a cyclist to cross so your photo has a bit of scale.
card.good_to_know: This was Bordeaux's first bridge, built between 1819 and 1822. It's 487 m long with 17 arches. Look for the pale medallions along the piers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Quai de Queyries on the right bank (rive droite) of the Garonne, in the Bastide district. Turn around and face back across the river at the bridge, with the Saint-Michel spire poking up past the far end.

card.hook: The church built its bell tower and then left it standing next to the building, like a very tall friend who wouldn't come inside. At 114 metres, it rules the Saint-Michel skyline.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Meynard, the square beside the Basilica of St. Michael. Face the bell tower as it rises over the open space.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the tower and the square together. Try 0.5x for more of the square and the church, then 2x to 5x to pick out details near the top of the tower (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright sky, then drag the slider down to make it a little darker, and the tower turns into a clean, dramatic silhouette.
card.best_time: Go at golden hour, when the low light gives the sky some colour behind the tower. A bright sky is what makes the silhouette work.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Place Meynard, in front of the basilica. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and stand with the basilica behind you, facing into the square, so the Flèche bell tower peeks over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot with the whole church and tower behind you, try Place de la Victoire, a square some distance away where both fit in the frame, and ask a passer-by to take it. Guides suggest mornings there, when the light is softer and it's less busy.
card.rules_and_safety: Place Meynard is an open public square, but the basilica is a place of worship, so be respectful during services. Photography inside may be restricted in some areas, so follow the signs and staff. One visitor says the street on the far side of the bridge is quiet after dark, so take a little care walking over then.
card.challenge: Line the tower up with a vertical gridline, hold the phone dead level, and see if you can make the tallest thing in Bordeaux stand up straight.
card.good_to_know: The basilica is Flamboyant Gothic, built between the end of the 14th century and the 16th century. The 114-metre bell tower dates from the 15th century and stands apart from the church. The basilica is also part of the Santiago de Compostela pilgrim routes World Heritage listing, along with two other Bordeaux churches. If you want to climb the tower, check it's open before you go.

card.hook: Bordeaux's bell tower stands apart from its cathedral on purpose, and that's good news for your photo: there's a whole open square to step back into. Tall, slim and topped with a steeple, it was made for a portrait-format shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Pey Berland, where the tower lies to the east, about 150 m away and roughly 2 minutes on foot. Face east toward it, with the cathedral beside it, and step back until the whole height fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower in from the square, then try 1x for a more natural look. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) is great for picking out the stonework and the steeple.
card.make_it_pop: Hold your phone upright, turn on the gridlines, and put the tower on one of the vertical lines with a little sky above the spire.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives the tower a lovely golden glow. Go early in the morning if you'd like the square quieter.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with a view, the official tower site invites visitors to snap one from the balcony of the second terrace, with the city behind you (the tower itself won't be in the shot). Use the front camera and keep your arm steady.
card.ask_someone: In Place Pey Berland, ask a passer-by to stand back in the square in front of the tower and beside the cathedral, while you pose with the tower in view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Climbing the tower is a separate timed visit with limited numbers, so check current opening before you go. The stairs are narrow stone spirals, so take care on the climb.
card.challenge: Can you get the whole tower in with the sides dead straight and a little sky above the spire? No leaning, no wobbly Pisa impression!
card.good_to_know: The tower was built between 1440 and 1500 on the initiative of Archbishop Pey Berland. It was kept apart from the cathedral so the vibrations of the bells wouldn't harm the main building. It has had an unusual past: first housing until 1790, then a lead factory, and its bells were only installed after 1851.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place Pey Berland, where the tower lies to the east, about 150 m away and roughly 2 minutes on foot. Face east toward it, with the cathedral beside it, and step back until the whole height fits.

card.hook: One park, three very different photos, and you can get all of them in a single wander. The Jardin Public gives you a wide green sweep, a formal terrace and a quiet pond with swans.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Jardin botanique de Bordeaux, on the botanical garden side of the park, and face across the park so the greenhouses sit in the background. To find the terrace and pond afterwards, walk west until they come into view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big view across the park. Switch to 0.5x on the terrace to fit in the flower beds, then try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the statues and the swans.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a line, then tap the greenhouses and drag the slider to make it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the greenery doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the greenery and the water, so aim for one of those if you can.
card.selfie_here: Try the arched green footbridge over the calm river. Use the front camera, stand on the bridge with the weeping willows and trees behind you, and try 0.5x to squeeze more garden into the frame. The bridge is only approximately placed, so check it on the map first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a little higher than you along the central alley (the allée principale), while you stand in the alley, so the symmetrical line of trees runs back behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public park, but check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and any restrictions on parts of the garden. The pond boat may not be running, so don't plan a shot around it.
card.challenge: Take one photo of each scene (park view, terrace, pond), then wait for a swan or duck to drift into the gap between the trees for bonus points.
card.good_to_know: The Jardin Public is a city park in Bordeaux. The Terrasse du Jardin public is a long formal terrace with flower beds, statues, a building along one edge and a basin in front. The Petit Pont is the small footbridge over the pond, with tree-lined banks and swans and ducks on the water.

card.hook: Most city halls look like they want to see your paperwork. The Palais Rohan just stands there in calm, pale stone with a clock in its pediment, waiting for you to step back and admire it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Pey-Berland, across the square from the main front, with the cathedral nearby. The palace is to the west of you, so face west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the postcard shot with the whole front and some open square. Go to 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out the clock and pediment. Use 0.5x when you're close up in the courtyard or the garden.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the central pediment up with the middle of the frame and keep your phone level so the tall lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is your best bet, because the facade gets warm light then.
card.selfie_here: Try the Jardin de la Mairie behind the palace: use the front camera at 0.5x with the back façade over your shoulder. The Cour d'honneur also works, with the palace behind you and the gate in front.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Place Pey-Berland to face the palace front with the cathedral on the far side of the square, while you stand in front of the facade, and ask them to step back to fit more in.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in public areas, but interior photography is restricted, so stick to the exterior and courtyard. Events can take place in the courtyard and temporary stands can block the square, so check the garden and courtyard are open when you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 2x and frame just the clock in the pediment, then see if a friend can guess which building it is.
card.good_to_know: The Palais Rohan was built as the archbishop's palace, commissioned in 1771 and finished in 1778. Napoleon and Louis XVIII both used it as a residence, and it became Bordeaux's city hall in 1835. The main gate has been replaced after damage, so recent photos may look different from older ones.

card.hook: Twelve statues stand on the roof of this opera house, and they've been looking down at Place de la Comédie for centuries. Nine are Muses, three are goddesses, and none of them ever complain about the crowds.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place de la Comédie, towards the right-hand side of the Grand Théâtre near the tram stop, with the theatre to the east of you. Face the building and you'll see all twelve columns and the statues above them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole front in. If you're close and the columns get cut off, drop to 0.5x. For the statues along the top, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then drag the slider to make the shot a touch darker so the sky stays blue and the columns keep their detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, around golden hour, is lovely because the low light picks out the columns and statues. If the front is lit up after dark, it's worth a few minutes, so switch on night mode and rest your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Go up the front steps of the Grand Théâtre with the colonnade behind you, ideally at golden hour. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the columns fit over your shoulder, or step in between the columns for a different look.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand to the right of the building beside the tram stop while you pose on the steps with the columns behind you (check the angle on the spot).
card.rules_and_safety: Trams run through this busy square, so watch your step while you wait for the perfect shot. The interior is guided tour only, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the full front, then wait for a tram to cross the frame and take another. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The Grand Théâtre opened on 17 April 1780, designed by Victor Louis as a temple to the arts. Its calm, symmetrical neoclassical front shows that. Today it's home to the Opéra National de Bordeaux and the Ballet National de Bordeaux.

card.hook: Most old churches make you crane your neck from a cramped street. Saint Severinus lets you stroll across a landscaped square and take a big, relaxed step back.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place des Martyrs-de-la-Résistance, about 1 minute on foot from the address, with the basilica to the north. Face north and you'll see the west-to-south side and the bell tower across the planting.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front and bell tower in, then 1x for a natural look. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tower top and the carvings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, and hold your phone level.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sun is behind or beside you rather than right over the tower. Check how the light falls when you arrive, and if the pale stone looks washed out, tap the church wall and slide a little darker.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Place des Martyrs de la Résistance, the square in front of the basilica, where reviewers praise the view. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the basilica fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back in the square, where the whole basilica fits in view, while you pose with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed inside except during services or where signs say otherwise. The church may be closed inside after a fire in the sacristy, so check the official site first if you want to go in. The outside views aren't affected.
card.challenge: Find the carving above the west door showing Saint Severinus and Saint Amand meeting, then see if you can count all fourteen carved figures on the south entrance.
card.good_to_know: Saint Severinus (Saint-Seurin in French) is one of three Bordeaux churches in the UNESCO Routes of Santiago de Compostela listing. It was rebuilt as a sturdy Romanesque church from the early 11th century, on ground used as a Christian burial place as far back as the 4th century. It was listed as a historic monument in 1840.

card.hook: Two square towers, a carved doorway and a big open square to back up into: this church practically begs you to step back and take the whole thing in.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Pierre Renaudel, the paved square in front of the church, and face the west front straight on. Use the paving as your foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so both towers and the doorway fit. Switch to 0.5x if the square is busy or you're close, and keep the façade in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for the carvings around the doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the middle of the doorway up with the centre line, and keep the phone level so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: The front probably looks warmest in the afternoon or early evening, but any soft daylight works. A quiet square makes it easier to get a clear view.
card.selfie_here: Stand in Place Pierre Renaudel with the Romanesque façade behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low, so the towers show up over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Place Pierre Renaudel, across from the church, while you stand with the façade behind you. Ask them to step back until both towers fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the square have sometimes been fenced off during works, so your view may be partly blocked. The church is open only at certain times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a passer-by to walk across the square and catch them tiny in front of the doorway, so the church looks huge.
card.good_to_know: This is a Romanesque church that once belonged to a Benedictine abbey founded in the 7th century. The building you see dates from the late 11th and early 12th centuries, and Paul Abadie restored it in the 19th century. The old abbey buildings now house the École des beaux-arts de Bordeaux.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place Pierre Renaudel, the paved square in front of the church, and face the west front straight on. Use the paving as your foreground.

card.hook: Imagine a bridge deck that lifts straight up like a lift, with two tall towers standing guard on either side. That's the Pont Jacques Chaban-Delmas, and yes, it's as fun to watch as it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand on Quai de Bacalan, on the left (Bacalan) bank at the bridge foot where the lift span rises. The bridge lies to the south-east, so face south-east with the river in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both towers, the deck and the river in one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to get close to the towers or the deck against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line one tower up with a vertical line so it stands nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or evening, when it's usually quieter. Check the lift schedule before you go: traffic stops when the deck rises, and the timing changes when ships pass. A raised deck makes a very different picture from a lowered one, so it's worth waiting for if you have time.
card.selfie_here: Try the Quai des Chartrons, the riverside quay along the Garonne in the Chartrons district, which a guide lists among Bordeaux's Instagram-friendly spots. Use the front camera at 0.5x and check on your screen that the bridge is over your shoulder before you tap, because we couldn't confirm the view from here.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Quai des Marques quayside, where the bridge is in view, to take your photo while you stand on the quay with the bridge behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: If you fancy the higher view from the Cité du Vin, check the official site before you go, as a ticket may be needed for the viewing level.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice from the same spot, once with the deck down and once with it up, then see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: The bridge opened on 16 March 2013. Its main span is 110 m long, and at the opening it was the longest vertical-lift bridge in Europe. It's named after Jacques Chaban-Delmas, a former Prime Minister of France and former mayor of Bordeaux.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Quai de Bacalan, on the left (Bacalan) bank at the bridge foot where the lift span rises. The bridge lies to the south-east, so face south-east with the river in front of you.
